tier_reason: The README at benchmark_url lists only absolute figures with no baseline. The linked peer-reviewed NSDI'19 paper does make comparative claims, but mostly against numbers published in other papers: ~10M vs ~1.5M 64 B RPCs/s per core against IX (quoted), 5.5 vs 9.7 us Raft replication against NetChain (published), and ~10x lower GET latency than Cell. The benchmark code (apps/small_rpc_tput, apps/large_rpc_tput, apps/latency, apps/smr) runs only eRPC, and the compiler is never named, so it cannot be A. Tier B is kept, but the win comes from comparisons across papers.

corrections.baseline: NSDI'19 paper baselines: FaSST RPCs and raw RDMA reads/writes (measured; eRPC is comparable but slightly slower), IX (per-core RPC rate quoted from the IX paper), NetChain and ZabFPGA replication (their published numbers), and the Cell RDMA B-tree (published numbers). The paper never benchmarks kernel TCP/UDP socket RPC or HERD.
corrections.claimed_speedup: NSDI'19 paper: one core handles ~10M small RPCs/s vs ~1.5M 64 B RPCs/s with IX (IX figure quoted, not re-measured; ~6.7x derived from page data). 3-way Raft replication takes 5.5 us median vs NetChain's published 9.7 us (~1.8x, derived from page data) and is 3% slower than ZabFPGA at the leader (3.1 vs 3.0 us). Masstree-over-eRPC median GET is 2.7 us, 'around 10x faster' than Cell's RDMA B-tree. Against its measured RDMA baselines eRPC is slightly slower: per-thread small-RPC rate up to 18% below FaSST, median latency up to 800 ns above RDMA reads, and at least 70% of RDMA-write bandwidth for requests of 32 kB or more (75 Gbps peak on one core). The README's absolute figures (2.3 us RTT, ~10M RPCs/s per core, 60-80M RPCs/s per NIC, 75 Gbps, 5.3 us Raft) have no baseline on that page. The paper gives 5.5 us, not 5.3 us, for Raft and does not contain the 60-80M per NIC figure.
corrections.hardware: NSDI'19 Table 1 lists three clusters. CX3: 11 nodes, 56 Gbps ConnectX-3 InfiniBand, Intel Xeon E5-2650 (8 cores). CX4: 100 CloudLab nodes, 25 GbE ConnectX-4 Lx lossy Ethernet, Xeon E5-2640 v4 (10 cores). CX5: 8 nodes, dual-port 40 GbE ConnectX-5, Xeon E5-2697 v3 (14 cores) or E5-2683 v4 (16 cores). Large-RPC bandwidth was measured between two CX5 nodes over 100 Gbps ConnectX-5 InfiniBand.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: The paper does not state them. The repo's CMakeLists.txt with the default PERF=ON uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE RelWithDebInfo plus -std=c++11 -march=native. The compiler is not named.
corrections.caveats: The paper's thesis is that eRPC is comparable to specialized systems while staying general. It never measures kernel TCP/UDP socket RPC or HERD, and against FaSST and raw RDMA it is slightly slower. Its 'faster' comparisons (IX, NetChain, Cell, and FaRM at scale) use numbers from other papers on different hardware; the authors say the NetChain comparison 'must be taken with a grain of salt'. The category fit is datacenter RPC over DPDK/RDMA rather than HTTP serving. The README's 5.3 us Raft and 60-80M RPCs/s per NIC figures are not in the paper, which gives 5.5 us. Authors now point new users to microsoft/machnet. The LICENSE file is the Apache-2.0 notice header (GitHub reports NOASSERTION).

notes: Metadata checked with gh: Apache-2.0 per the LICENSE file, not archived, not a fork, 907 stars, last commit 2024-05-09, so stale is correct. Tier stays B, but the verdict is downgrade because the record's baseline (kernel TCP/UDP RPC, FaSST/HERD) misstates the paper: it never benchmarks kernel sockets or HERD, and eRPC loses slightly to FaSST.

tier_reason: The peer-reviewed NSDI'22 paper measures FlexTOE head-to-head against the Linux kernel TCP stack, TAS and the Chelsio T6 TOE on the same testbed (Xeon Gold 6138 hosts) and shows wins. It is not A: the repo has no benchmark code (no memtier/RPC benchmark directory) and the host compiler and flags are never stated (only 'NFP compiler toolchain 6.1.0.1' for the SmartNIC firmware).

corrections.claimed_speedup: From the abstract, arXiv 2110.10919 and NSDI'22 alike: Memcached scales up to 38% better than TAS and saves up to 81% of host CPU cycles vs Chelsio. 99.99th-percentile RPC RTT is 3.2x lower than Chelsio and 50% lower than TAS. Single-connection RPC throughput is up to 2.4x TAS on x86 and 4x TAS on BlueField. The full paper's Linux-kernel-TCP figures: Memcached throughput up to 5.5x Linux, 4.9x Chelsio and 1.6x TAS (Fig. 8). RPC throughput at 250 cycles/RPC is up to 4x Linux and 5.3x Chelsio when receiving, and over 7.6x Linux and Chelsio when sending (Fig. 10). With up to 2K connections it reaches 3.3x Linux. FlexTOE loses in some cases: median small-RPC latency is 20 us vs 14 us for Chelsio and 16 us for TAS, and TAS is 1.5x better in the connection-scalability benchmark.
corrections.hardware: Two 20-core Intel Xeon Gold 6138 @ 2 GHz servers (40 GB RAM), each with a Netronome Agilio CX40 40 Gbps, a Chelsio Terminator T62100-LP-CR 100 Gbps and an Intel XL710 40 Gbps NIC. Extra clients: two 2x18-core Xeon Gold 6154 @ 3 GHz (ConnectX-5 100 Gbps) and two 4-core Xeon E3-1230 v5 @ 3.4 GHz (82599ES 10 Gbps), on a 100 Gbps switch. The generalization runs used a Mellanox BlueField MBF1M332A-ASCAT 25 Gbps SmartNIC and a 32-core AMD EPYC 7452 @ 2.35 GHz host with a ConnectX-5 100 Gbps NIC.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: SmartNIC firmware was built with the NFP compiler toolchain 6.1.0.1. The host compiler and flags are not stated.
corrections.caveats: FlexTOE needs a Netronome Agilio (NFP-4000/6000) SmartNIC and 1G hugepages; the x86 and BlueField ports are described in the paper's appendix E but no separate port or benchmark directory is visible in the repo tree. It trades median latency for tail latency and throughput (20 us median vs 14-16 us for Chelsio/TAS), and TAS beats it by 1.5x on connection scalability. TAS ran on an Intel XL710 because of a slow Agilio DPDK driver. The category fit is a TCP offload engine rather than an HTTP server. The TAS baseline is an academic stack; the Linux kernel TCP stack is the recognizable incumbent (up to 5.5x Memcached throughput).

notes: The abstract numbers are exact on arXiv and in the NSDI'22 PDF (both opened). benchmark_url now points at the full NSDI PDF, which also holds the Linux-baseline figures. gh confirms BSD-3-Clause, not archived, not a fork, 62 stars, last commit 2022-02-27, so abandoned is correct.

tier_reason: The peer-reviewed OSDI'14 Best Paper measures IX against Linux 3.16.1 and mTCP on the same cluster. Its abstract gives up to 3.6x key-value-store (memcached) throughput and more than 2x lower tail latency. The compiler and flags are never stated and no benchmark harness sits in the repo, so it is not A. This matches the earlier verification of the same paper and repo at tier B.

corrections.baseline: Linux 3.16.1 kernel TCP stack (Ubuntu 14.04) and mTCP, a user-level TCP stack run on Linux 2.6.36
corrections.hardware: Server: Intel Xeon E5-2665 @ 2.4 GHz with 256 GB DRAM. 24 clients: a mix of Xeon E5-2637 @ 3.5 GHz and E5-2650 @ 2.6 GHz (8 cores/16 hyperthreads per socket). All machines use Intel x520 (82599EB) 10GbE NICs on a Quanta/Cumulus 48x10GbE switch (Broadcom Trident+); the server runs 1x10GbE or 4x10GbE bonded.

notes: Duplicate of an entry already verified (OSDI'14, github.com/ix-project/ix, tier B); this quick check is consistent with it. The presentation page and full PDF confirm 3.6x memcached throughput vs Linux at a given 99th-percentile latency bound and more than 2x lower tail latency. gh confirms 136 stars, last commit 2017-11-06 (abandoned), not archived or a fork, and a LICENSE titled 'IX Open Source License' whose text is verbatim MIT.
